archetype.name: Improviser (accurate from the pocket)
archetype.definition: A third-year QB who still holds the ball to extend plays and scramble for first downs, but who now pairs that freelance streak with some of the cleanest ball placement in the league.

report.headline: The accuracy leap is real; the touchdowns haven't caught up yet.
report.take:
Caleb Williams has always been a play-extender. His time to throw sits at 3.24 seconds, essentially last year's 3.2, and his aggressiveness has barely moved (11.39% vs 11.3%). He still buys time, still scrambles, and still takes sacks while hunting for something better. What has changed is the throw itself. Last season he completed 58.1% with a CPOE of -3.5 and a bad-throw rate of 17.8%. This year he is at 70.9%, a CPOE of 7.2 (5th of 47), and a bad-throw rate of 8.9%, the lowest among 38 charted passers. Same style, much better delivery. That is the season.

The efficiency follows from it. His 0.289 EPA per dropback ranks 6th and sits far above the league average of 0.034. He has thrown one interception in 158 attempts and lost no fumbles. The damage comes in the 10-to-19-yard window: 0.767 EPA per attempt on 33 throws, the most valuable depth he has. Rome Odunze has been the main beneficiary at 1.101 EPA per target. Ben Johnson's offense also feeds him plenty of layups, with 34 throws behind the line completed at 88.2%. His intended air yards (6.93) are shorter than last year's 8.4 aDOT. Some of the completion jump is therefore structural, but CPOE controls for depth, and that is where he has improved most.

The numbers hide two things that pull in opposite directions. His TD rate of 3.8% ranks only 28th and trails the league's 4.6%, which is the main reason his 253.4 passing yards a game outpace his 1.2 TDs. That should correct; he threw 27 touchdowns last year and has been efficient in the red zone. The sacks are the other side. A 7.6% sack rate ranks 29th, and 30.8% of his pressures end in sacks. That falls between his rookie mess (43.5%) and last year's excellent 15.9%. It is the cost of holding the ball, and his 15 scrambles at 0.681 EPA apiece repay a lot of it. His designed runs (-0.802 EPA, 62.5% stuffed) do not.

The last three weeks, all wins, look like the season, only busier: 286.7 yards a game, 9.05 adjusted net yards per dropback, no picks, with his own rushing fading to 7.3 yards a game. The one real failure came in Week 2 against Minnesota, now the league's top-ranked defense. He was pressured on 40.6% of dropbacks and finished at -1.0 EPA. That game is the test case for this week.

strengths.title: Rebuilt accuracy and ball placement
strengths.body: His CPOE has swung from -3.5 to 7.2 and his bad-throw rate has halved to the best mark among charted passers. His timing and aggressiveness are unchanged, so this is not just a switch to safer throws. It is a better throw on the same kind of play. Some CPOE regression is normal over 158 attempts, but a drop in bad throws this large usually reflects mechanics and tends to stick.

strengths.title: Intermediate window drives the offense
strengths.body: Throws of 10-19 air yards return 0.767 EPA each despite a 54.5% completion rate. They are high-value strikes, with Odunze the main target. This is the skill that separates a top-10 efficiency QB from a checkdown manager. At 33 attempts it is the split most likely to cool, but even a sizable pullback leaves it a clear plus.

strengths.title: Scrambles that pay for themselves
strengths.body: His 15 scrambles average 0.681 EPA and produced seven first downs. That is why holding the ball makes sense for him even with the sacks. Off-script creation has been his trait since he entered the league, so it is durable.

concerns.title: Sacks are the tax on extension
concerns.body: A 7.6% sack rate ranks 29th, and 30.8% of pressures become sacks. That is well off last year's 15.9% but far better than his rookie 43.5%. It comes from the same 3.2-plus-second clock that produces his scrambles. That makes it a cost of his style more than a pocket flaw, but it lives on against defenses that can get home.

concerns.title: Touchdown rate trails the efficiency
concerns.body: He is 6th in EPA per dropback but 28th in TD rate. His TD rate is below the league average even though he has been sharp in the red zone. This looks like small-sample distribution rather than a red-zone problem, and it is more likely to rise than to stay this low.

concerns.title: Designed runs are dead plays
concerns.body: Called runs return -0.802 EPA with 62.5% stuffed. His rushing value has come entirely from scrambles, and his rushing output has dropped sharply over the last three games. Don't count on his legs as a fantasy floor unless the scrambles come back.

trend.note: After the Week 2 dud against Minnesota, the three games since his return in Week 6 have matched his season efficiency almost exactly (0.287 EPA per dropback vs 0.289) with more passing volume. That includes 7.7 EPA in a road win at fifth-ranked Seattle.

nextGame.headline: Elite coverage, soft rush: a test of his patience
nextGame.body:
Tampa Bay brings the league's second-best pass defense by EPA and the second-stingiest short-area defense. It holds quarterbacks to 11.6 PPR a game, third-fewest. That runs straight at his quick game and his intermediate timing. The softer spots are the pass rush and the deep zone. The Bucs rank 28th in hit rate and 24th in sack rate, which shrinks his biggest weakness and gives his 3-plus-second clock room to work. They are only 19th against deep passes. That rewards exactly the extended plays he likes, and Tampa's WR2s have run well over their averages. Their offense is 30th in pass EPA, and the Bears are 6-point home favorites. A lead is the likely script, and his EPA turns negative when Chicago is up nine or more, so late volume could be capped.

Williams practiced fully on his last report and is active. The Bears' only meaningful absence is backup back Kyle Monangai (41% of snaps), which should push more work to D'Andre Swift, a useful checkdown. On Tampa's side, Yaya Diaby (53% of snaps) is out with an MCL sprain and Christian Rozeboom is on IR. Both losses thin a rush that already struggles to get home. Emeka Egbuka's absence hurts the Bucs' offense and makes a Chicago lead more likely.

keyMatchups.title: His clock against a weak rush
keyMatchups.body: Tampa rarely hits or sacks quarterbacks, and Diaby's absence thins that further. If Williams gets clean pockets, his long time to throw becomes an asset rather than a sack risk. His Week 2 collapse came at a 40.6% pressure rate, which is not this defense's profile.

keyMatchups.title: Short game into a wall
keyMatchups.body: Tampa is second against short passes, where Williams throws most of his volume. The easy completions that propped up his 70.9% may dry up. His production will lean on the deeper throws, where the Bucs are merely average.

keyMatchups.title: Lead script caps the ceiling
keyMatchups.body: With Tampa's offense near the bottom in passing efficiency, Chicago could build a margin early. Williams has been flat when leading by nine or more. A comfortable win may come with a modest stat line.

nextGame.watch: Whether he hits throws beyond 10 air yards against a top coverage unit that can't pressure him. That separates a Seattle-type game from a Minnesota one.

restOfSeason.body:
The core of this season should hold. The bad-throw rate and CPOE gains came without any change in how long he holds the ball or how aggressive he is, which points to a better passer rather than a friendlier menu. Expect the completion rate to settle in the mid-to-high 60s and the intermediate EPA to cool from its current spike. Even so, he projects as a top-10 efficiency quarterback in an offense that ranks 6th in success rate. His 4,308-yard pace looks reasonable, and I'd expect touchdowns to rise toward 1.4-1.8 a game as his TD rate catches up to his efficiency and red-zone play.

The soft spots are sacks and rushing. His pressure-to-sack rate will swing with opponent pass rushes, and his rushing has shrunk to scrambles only. Plan on roughly 12-25 rushing yards a game, not the Week 1 explosion. The bigger risk is defenses like Minnesota that can both cover and pressure. He has faced only one, and it went badly.
swingFactors: How he handles defenses that can generate pressure
Whether the TD rate normalizes to his efficiency
Odunze sustaining his intermediate and deep production

confidence.note: Five games and 158 attempts, but the accuracy gain shows up across every depth and direction.
